title: Nidhanapataye namaḥ: the names used in installing a liṅga
theme: Twenty-two names of Śiva in pairs — the god and his liṅga — with which, the text says, the liṅga of all is installed.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «नितरां बहूनि धनानि निधनानि तेषां पतिः कुबेररूपेण तस्मै» — lord of abundant wealth, as Kubera

words.meaning: to the near one who guards treasure
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «निधनपश्चासौ तश्चेति निधनपतः», and «भक्तानां समीपत्वादन्तिकः» — near to his devotees
The anonymous commentator: «हिरण्यलिङ्गाय कनकनिर्मितलिङ्गाकाराय» — in the form of a liṅga made of gold
The anonymous commentator: «सुवर्णलिङ्गाय रजतनिर्मितलिङ्गाकाराय» — of silver, as he reads suvarṇa here

sandhi.rule: Each name ends in a vowel before n: the words stand side by side; namaḥ before the pause keeps its visarga.

samasa.meaning: lord of treasures (or, read otherwise, lord of the end)

morphology.note: nidhana usually means ‘end, death’; the anonymous commentator reads it as ni + dhana, ‘abundant wealth’, and the lord as Kubera’s form. The text gives no gloss.
Analysed by the anonymous commentator as nidhana-pa + ta + antika: ‘guardian of treasure’, ‘who spreads [it] to devotees’, and ‘near’ — a learned etymology of an unusual word.

translation.literal: To the lord of treasures, homage. To the near one, guardian of treasure, homage. To the one on high, homage. To the liṅga on high, homage. To the golden one, homage. To the golden liṅga, homage. To the bright-coloured one, homage. To the bright-coloured liṅga, homage. To the heavenly one, homage. To the heavenly liṅga, homage.
translation.readable: Homage to the lord of treasures, and to the near one who guards them. Homage to the one on high and to the liṅga on high; to the golden one and the golden liṅga; to the bright one and the bright liṅga; to the heavenly one and the heavenly liṅga.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «शृणाति प्रलये ब्रह्माण्डं हिनस्तीति शर्वस्तस्मै» — who destroys the world-egg at the dissolution
The anonymous commentator: «ज्वललिङ्गाय भूलोके विद्यमानद्वादशज्योतिर्लिङ्गरूपाय» — as the twelve jyotirliṅgas on earth
The anonymous commentator: «आत्माय निखिलजगदात्मकाय» — the self of the whole world

words.meaning: to the liṅga of the self

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «यस्मादुत्कृष्टो नास्ति स परमस्तस्मै» — than whom there is none higher
The anonymous commentator: «पाण्युपलक्षितसर्वावयवायमाना मन्त्रा वेदवाक्यविशेषा यस्य तत्पाणिमन्त्रम्», «त्रयीमयशरीरमिति यावत्» — whose body is the three Vedas

sandhi.rule: etat + somasya → etat somasya (no change; written together).
sarvaliṅgam + sthāpayati → sarvaliṅgaṃ sthāpayati (P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः)); the recitation writes this anusvāra before a sibilant as ग्ग्.

morphology.note: An a-stem dative made from ātman (for the regular ātmane), as the list’s rhythm of -āya datives requires.
The base writes सर्वलिङ्गग्ग्, the Taittirīya recitation’s spelling of the anusvāra before s; the other witnesses write ँ or ꣳ.

translation.literal: To Bhava, homage; to the liṅga of Bhava, homage; to Śarva, homage; to the liṅga of Śarva, homage; to Śiva, homage; to the liṅga of Śiva, homage; to the blazing one, homage; to the blazing liṅga, homage; to the self, homage; to the liṅga of the self, homage; to the highest, homage; to the highest liṅga, homage. [With] this, [one] sets up the liṅga of all, of Soma, of Sūrya — [the liṅga] whose limbs are mantras, purifying.
translation.readable: Homage to Bhava and the liṅga of Bhava; to Śarva and his liṅga; to Śiva and his liṅga; to the blazing one and the blazing liṅga; to the self and the liṅga of the self; to the highest and the highest liṅga. With these one installs the liṅga that belongs to all — to the moon and the sun — a purifying liṅga whose limbs are the mantras.

syntax: A litany of datives with namaḥ, arranged in pairs: a name of the god and the same name with liṅga (‘to Bhava, to Bhava’s liṅga’). The last line is a sentence of a different kind, a brāhmaṇa-like statement of use: etat (‘this’) … sthāpayati (‘[one] sets up’), with sarvaliṅgam as object, qualified by the genitives somasya sūryasya and by pāṇimantram pavitram.

ambiguities.note: nidhana ordinarily means ‘end, death’, so ‘lord of the end’ is a possible reading; the anonymous commentator reads ‘lord of treasures’, as Kubera’s form. No other commentary on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources.

Since gold (hiraṇya) has just been named, the anonymous commentator takes suvarṇa here as silver, by etymology (‘of fine colour’): «हिरण्यस्योक्तत्वात्सुवर्णशब्दो रूढिमुत्सृज्य योगेन रजतं वदति». The text itself may simply repeat ‘gold’ in another word.
Who sets up the liṅga is not said; the commentator supplies the worshipper. somasya sūryasya may qualify the liṅga as belonging to the moon and the sun, or, as he takes it, stand for all the deities.

metre.name: prose
metre.note: A yajus litany: the name-lines count 5 to 10 syllables (8, 10, 5, 7, 6, 8, 6, 8, 5, 7 in the first unit; 5, 7, … 6, 8 in the second), and the last line 23.

beginner: This section is a list of names of Śiva, given in pairs: first the god under a name, then his liṅga — the simple upright stone or metal form in which Śiva is worshipped — under the same name. So: homage to the golden one, homage to the golden liṅga; to Śiva, and to the liṅga of Śiva; to the highest, and to the highest liṅga. The final line says what these names are for: with them one installs ‘the liṅga of all’. The old anonymous commentator says the mantras are used when a liṅga is set up in a new temple, or each day when a clay liṅga is made for worship. He also explains some puzzling words, taking ‘suvarṇa’ here as silver because gold has already been named. The text describes a rite; it makes no promise about results.
analogy: Like the words spoken at the laying of a foundation stone, naming both the building and the one it is built for.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It offers homage to the god under ten names in the first unit and twelve in the second, each paired with the liṅga of that name, and says that with these one installs the liṅga of all, of Soma and Sūrya, whose limbs are mantras, purifying.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: when a liṅga is installed in a newly built Śiva temple and daily when a clay liṅga is installed, «इतः परं नूतनशिवालयादिकं कृत्वा तत्र लिङ्गप्रतिष्ठापनावसरे प्रत्यहं पार्थिवलिङ्गप्रतिष्ठापनावसरे च विनियुक्ता»; he takes this from the mantra’s own words, «सर्वलिङ्गँ स्थापयति». He also says they are for homage to Pārvatī’s lord and for removing sin by recitation alone; that is his claim about their use, not the text’s.

commentary.q: How does he read the liṅgas?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: As forms the god takes in the worlds: the liṅga on high worshipped by the gods in the upper worlds, «ऊर्ध्वायोर्ध्वलोकेषु देवतारूपेण विद्यमानायेत्यर्थः»; liṅgas of gold and silver; the blazing liṅga as the twelve jyotirliṅgas on earth, «ज्वललिङ्गाय भूलोके विद्यमानद्वादशज्योतिर्लिङ्गरूपाय».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: the liṅga whose limbs, of which the hand stands for all, are the Vedic mantras, «पाण्युपलक्षितसर्वावयवायमाना मन्त्रा वेदवाक्यविशेषा यस्य तत्पाणिमन्त्रम्» — in short, whose body is the three Vedas, «त्रयीमयशरीरमिति यावत्».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The commentator says every member of the three twice-born classes installs it; that restriction is his gloss, not the text’s, which names no one.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not available here), and no comment by Sāyaṇa or Bhāskara on these names is in the edition’s copies. The anonymous commentator reads them as a rite of installing the liṅga.

contemporary.text: Each name is given twice, once for the god and once for the form in which he is worshipped. The pairing keeps in view that the visible object and what it stands for are both honoured, and are not simply the same. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Why might a list name both the god and his liṅga each time?
reflect.deeper: The commentator gives learned etymologies for difficult words (nidhanapata, suvarṇa). When is an etymology an explanation, and when a new meaning?
reflect.practice: Choose an object that stands for something you value, and say plainly what it stands for.

references.text: No Sāyaṇa or Bhāskara comment on this anuvāka is in the copies used; the anonymous commentator’s is the only one.

flags.note: The text writes सर्वलिङ्गग्ग् (the recitation’s anusvāra before s); the checker must read ग्ग् before a sibilant as anusvāra for the padaccheda to rejoin — reported as a shared-code need.
nidhanapati as ‘lord of treasures’ and suvarṇa as ‘silver’ are the anonymous commentator’s readings.
Only one commentary on this anuvāka is available.
